title: Tanker Freight Goes Tenfold: Asian Refiners Cut US Crude Orders by Half as the Gulf Shuttle Fleet Eats the World's VLCCs
subhead: Shipping crude from the US Gulf Coast to Asia now costs up to $80 million a voyage, ten times pre-war rates. Asia's November orders for US crude have halved to about 25 million barrels, and Europe's gas benchmark has hit its highest level since December 2022.

sections.heading: The shipping crisis is now doing more damage than the supply crisis
sections.body:
Crude has been flowing out of the Persian Gulf again — but it is arriving through a bottleneck of ships, not pipelines. According to Bloomberg data cited by Oilprice.com, the cost of moving a supertanker of crude from the US Gulf Coast to China peaked at $80 million earlier this month, roughly ten times the rate that held for years before the Iran war. It has since eased to about $60 million per voyage, still far above anything the market has absorbed before.

The mechanism is the Gulf of Oman shuttle. Middle East producers are moving barrels out of Hormuz by ship-to-ship transfers offshore Oman, and the shuttle fleet has grown to about 80 VLCCs, per Kpler data. Those vessels are tied up for weeks waiting for transfers, which starves every other long-haul route of tonnage. The result is that Asian refiners have cut orders for US crude by roughly 50% month-on-month, to about 25 million barrels for November delivery — potentially Asia's lowest intake of US crude in seven years, according to vessel-tracking analysts.

The distortion shows up in the price structure as well. Singapore's high-sulphur fuel oil crack against Dubai crude jumped above $10 per barrel in mid-October from a $5 discount in February — a $15 swing for a product that is normally worth less than the crude it comes from. The Singapore–Rotterdam HSFO swap spread hit a record $95 per tonne on October 7 before easing to $88. Europe-to-Asia voyages for HSFO now cost roughly $36 per barrel, over five times last year's level.

Replacement barrels are also thinning. Middle Eastern HSFO and VLSFO shipments to Singapore averaged about 100,000 b/d in 2025, fell away in April and May, briefly recovered to 130,000 b/d in July, and are back to 40,000–50,000 b/d. Russia filled the gap briefly at 180,000 b/d in April, but Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries cut those flows to 25,000 b/d by September.
sections.whyItMatters: Two supply sources failed at once and the freight market cannot substitute for either. The war's cost is now being transmitted through logistics rather than barrels — which is why prices stay high even as Gulf export volumes recover.

sections.heading: The paper market and the cargo market have decoupled again — this time in the other direction
sections.body:
Brent settled around $114 on Friday and has been trading near $114.60, with WTI near $101. Yet physical Middle Eastern crude is selling at a widening discount. Iraq's Basrah Medium was recently done at a $10 per barrel discount to Dubai, from near parity a month earlier, traders told Bloomberg. The Oman–Dubai differential — the region's key measure of physical strength — has fallen to its lowest since the end of July, after spiking as high as $65 per barrel in March when Hormuz was effectively shut.

The split is straightforward once you separate the two books. The futures market is pricing an escalation that has not happened — ING strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey note reports that Trump is considering fresh strikes on Iran and that the US is deploying a second aircraft carrier to the region. The physical market is pricing the barrels that are actually moving through the shuttle system. One is a probability, the other is a fact.

Also worth flagging: the weekly EIA data shows US commercial crude inventories fell by 3.1 million barrels in the week to October 16, so the tightness is not purely a Gulf story.
sections.whyItMatters: When futures and physicals diverge this sharply, one of them is wrong. Either an escalation arrives and the physical discount was mispriced, or the risk premium bleeds out of Brent. The second aircraft carrier suggests the market is not being paranoid.

sections.heading: US diesel at $6.32 a gallon forces Washington onto the SPR — and to Moscow
sections.body:
The US average diesel price stood at $6.3172 per gallon on October 23, against $3.63 a year earlier. That is an election problem, and the administration is answering it with emergency stock and Russian barrels.

On October 23 the Department of Energy authorised an emergency exchange of up to 400,000 barrels to Phillips 66's Lake Charles refinery, drawing on the West Hackberry site in Louisiana, citing a temporary disruption to crude deliveries. It was the second such authorisation this month: on October 10, DOE released up to 4 million barrels for ExxonMobil and BP after weather-related disruptions. Phillips 66 must return the barrels plus a premium.

The reserve cannot carry much more of this. The SPR held 282.7 million barrels as of the latest DOE figure — its lowest level since October 1982, according to Reuters data. It entered the Iran war having rebuilt only about a quarter of the 180 million barrels sold after Russia's 2022 invasion, and DOE's refill math runs about six times slower than its drawdown rate, with some returns not due until late 2028. DOE puts a full refill at roughly $20 billion against $171 million Congress has appropriated.

On the supply side, the first Russian diesel cargo under the Trump–Putin deal left Primorsk on October 23 aboard the Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes — about 300,000 barrels of ultra-low-sulphur diesel, bound for New York with an expected arrival of November 7. That is four days after the midterms, and analysts quoted by Oilprice.com say the volumes are too small to move a global diesel market this tight. Two other Russian diesel cargoes have signalled Turkey and Brazil, per LSEG data cited by Reuters.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington is drawing down a strategic reserve that is already at its 1982 floor to solve refinery-level logistics, while its political answer to diesel prices arrives after the vote it was meant to influence. Neither lever is scalable.

sections.heading: European gas at €92/MWh: storage peaked at 75% and Qatar is still offline
sections.body:
TTF, Europe's gas benchmark, settled above €90 per MWh on Thursday and topped €92 on Friday morning — $103.40 per MWh, equivalent to over $30 per MMBtu, and the highest since December 2022, when Europe faced its first winter without most Russian pipeline gas.

The cause is arithmetic, not sentiment. Qatari LNG flows remain restricted by the Middle East escalation, and EU storage was only 74.62% full as of October 22 per Gas Infrastructure Europe, against a five-year average of about 86% for this point in the year — a gap of more than ten percentage points heading into the heating season. Some member states have already begun drawing down.

ING is explicit that storage appears to have peaked just under 75%, and that LNG is 'increasingly likely to be largely absent from the market for at least much of the Northern Hemisphere winter.' That leaves Europe going into winter with a structural hole it cannot fill from the spot market at any reasonable price.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe is entering winter with a ten-point storage deficit and its largest LNG supplier effectively unavailable. Whatever happens in Hormuz over the next six weeks, Europe's gas price will be set by tanker schedules, not by storage policy.

sections.heading: Iran's Hormuz claims meet a US counter-claim, and both sides are talking to their own audiences
sections.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed on Thursday that seven oil tankers were struck in the Strait of Hormuz — four hit while transferring oil and set alight overnight, three disabled by mines. Al Jazeera reported it could not independently verify the claims, and the IRGC did not identify flags or casualties. The IRGC warned it could strike US bases in the region if Washington escorts tankers through other parts of the strait: 'The US military must know that if this trend continues, the conflict will extend to its bases in the region.'

A US Central Command spokesperson told Al Jazeera the mine claims are incorrect, that US forces have cleared the international lanes, that Iran is using missiles and drones instead, and that 95% of vessels are still getting through. President Trump posted on Truth Social that Iran is 'making up fake hits, mines, and everything else' to lift oil prices before the midterms, and that more oil is transiting Hormuz now than before the conflict.

Al Jazeera's Tehran correspondent reports talk in the Iranian capital of an expected US strike before the November midterms, with the IRGC army chief claiming Iran has produced enough equipment to fight a symmetrical war. Separately, RFE/RL reporting carried by Oilprice.com notes that Iranian hardliners are now openly discussing nuclear weapons, breaking a long taboo anchored in Khamenei's fatwa.

The volume data is genuinely contested. A Wall Street Journal report citing Kpler put total Middle East flows in the week to October 18 at 24 million b/d — above pre-war levels — while Reuters cited Kpler estimating Hormuz flows specifically at 8.5 million b/d, against the WSJ's 14 million b/d. That gap is the whole argument.
sections.whyItMatters: Both sides are now managing expectations for an escalation they each say the other will start. The Kpler discrepancy matters more than either press statement: nobody outside the strait has a reliable count of what is actually moving.

sections.heading: Chevron moves on West Qurna as Washington reorders Iraq
sections.body:
Chevron is moving to take over Russia's most prized Iraqi oil field, according to reporting by Simon Watkins for Oilprice.com. The company signed four preliminary agreements with Iraq's Oil Ministry in February, and the West Qurna move signals that Washington intends to convert military position into equity in Iraq's upstream.

This is the quieter half of the war's energy story. While tankers and pipelines dominate the headlines, the ownership of Iraqi production capacity is being renegotiated — and the beneficiary is a US major displacing a Russian operator. The same logic runs through the Venezuela file, where the private US partner in the administration's production deal has added about 20,000 b/d since August.
sections.whyItMatters: Iraq's southern fields are one of the few large supply sources outside Hormuz's immediate reach. Who operates them determines whose barrels reach Asia when the strait is degraded — and Chevron taking Russian position is a durable shift, not a trading position.

sections.heading: Asia is building the next energy market on its own terms — coal included
sections.body:
McKinsey estimates Asia will account for about 70% of global net energy demand growth through 2040 and needs $1 trillion a year in energy investment over the next 15 years, according to analysis carried by Oilprice.com. Regional energy demand is now projected at 370 million terajoules, a 15% increase over last year's forecast, driven by data centres, industrial expansion and cooling.

The composition matters more than the total. Coal is about 47% of Asia's primary energy mix, oil 25% and gas roughly 12%, and coal supplies over 50% of Asia's electricity — 67% in South Asia, led by India. Coal use is expected to decline slowly in China as renewables scale, but rising Indian and Southeast Asian demand is projected to hold the regional total steady. Asian thermal coal prices remain elevated on reduced Chinese output, Indonesian supply quotas, and gas-to-coal switching in Japan and South Korea.

The one thing that could change the arithmetic: McKinsey projects biofuels could displace up to $100 billion in annual fuel imports by 2040, with India and Indonesia expanding blending mandates.
sections.whyItMatters: A war that has made oil and gas expensive is accelerating Asia's pivot to coal and domestic alternatives, not to the transition Washington and Brussels describe. The continent's import bill is the lever, and it is being pulled hard.

bottomLine: The Gulf is exporting crude again and it does not matter, because there are not enough ships to carry it where it needs to go. Freight from the US Gulf to Asia at $60–80 million a voyage has halved Asia's appetite for American barrels, blown out Singapore's fuel oil market, and left Brent at $114 while Iraqi crude sells at a $10 discount. The US is answering a $6.32 diesel price with a Strategic Petroleum Reserve already at its lowest since 1982, and with Russian cargoes that arrive four days after the midterms. Europe is going into winter with storage at 75% and Qatari LNG unavailable, gas at €92/MWh and rising. Watch three things this week: whether the second US carrier group turns a risk premium into an actual escalation, whether Asian refiners keep cutting US orders into December, and whether the Kpler flow numbers reconcile — because right now the market is trading two different wars.
sources: Oilprice.com, Bloomberg, Reuters, Al Jazeera, ING (Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey), Kpler, Gas Infrastructure Europe (AGSI), US Department of Energy, US Energy Information Administration, AAA, LSEG, Kommersant, Wall Street Journal, McKinsey, RFE/RL, Eurasianet
